title: Lawfare Daily: Aya Ibrahim on Progressive Priorities for the New Democratic Congress
content:
In this episode of the Security Economics podcast series, Peter Harrell and AI Now’s Aya Ibrahim discuss the agenda for the next Congress, AI regulation, and U.S.-China policy.

Aya joins Lawfare Contributing Editor and host of the Security Economics podcast Peter Harrell to talk about a progressive agenda for the next Congress, about AI regulation, and about U.S.-China policy. Aya and Peter also look back at things that the Biden Administration got right—and wrong—about U.S.-China competition, and they close by talking about how to balance security economics with the domestic economy. 

This episode is part of the Security Economics podcast series, in which Peter Harrell and guests explore the intersection of economics and national security, how countries manage their economies to support national security, and how they deploy economic tools in support of geopolitical objectives. 

Listen to the full episode here.

title: AI Now Statement on the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA) to US Congress
content:
The AI Now Institute has released a statement outlining concerns with the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BAAJA), which serves as a backdoor bailout of the AI industry. The statement’s key points are as follows:

  • BAAJA is a vote for a “backdoor bailout” of the AI industry.
  • BAAJA preempts the few levers that local, state, and Tribal authorities have to hold Big Tech accountable.
  • BAAJA supercharges AI data center expansion in exchange for token ratepayer protections.

    • Last week, voters across the country made their position clear by rejecting the AI buildout and electing representatives who are championing data center moratoria. Now, Congress has a choice to make: do the bidding of Silicon Valley and special interests or stand with local communities working to shape their own futures.

title: The AI Safety Debate Has Lost the Plot. We Asked 10 Experts What the Real Nightmares Are
content:
How should people think about AI safety?
Some of the comparisons that people draw between AI and nuclear are quite frustrating. Despite constantly comparing AI to nuclear, they’re denying standard risk assessment techniques as being sufficient to control AI. I wrote an entire paper on this.

Part of this field of risk assessment was born out of the Manhattan Project. Scientists were very concerned, and they developed rigorous standards around systems to limit harm to human life, the environment, and even financial and national security assets. They came up with methods for assessing safety that were ultimately based on answering a democratic question: How safe is safe enough? That is the question that any safety engineer has to ask, and is core to everything that follows.

content:

content:

title: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
content:
In a new essay, [OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris] Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order.

[…]

Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure. 

“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.” 

Read the full article here.

title: Who will get to define the danger?
content:
Webster Hall in Manhattan has a long history of rebellion. A century ago, garment workers organised strikes here, socialists debated the future, and New York’s radicals gathered to demand change.

On October 19, the grand ballroom was packed again. The crowd, spilling onto the balconies, laughed at Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s jokes, cheered former antitrust chief Lina Khan, and hung on the every word of writers Arundhati Roy, Karen Hao and Naomi Klein. The cause that brought them together? Artificial intelligence.

title: COP31 pledge on AI lacks climate targets, critics say
content:
The pledge doesn’t acknowledge the link with fossil fuels, even as the data center boom threatens tech companies’ pledges to reduce planet-warming emissions. Some experts worry that part of the pledge plays into an industry narrative, which asserts that data center impacts can be mitigated by using AI to address climate change.

“We have seen over many, many years that voluntary pledges are not enough and that self-regulation by industry does not work — we can’t trust them to grade their own homework,” said Alli Finn, head of community partnerships at AI Now Institute, a nonprofit that studies the societal effects of AI.

Read the full article here.

title: What Should the Rules for A.I. Companies Actually Be? We Asked the Experts.
content:
What should the government do? We asked a panel of experts to assess the risks A.I. presents and the tools of governance that could be adopted to address them.

Kate Brennan, a former Google tech worker, leads the policy agenda on A.I. and corporate power at the AI Now Institute, an independent research institute providing expert analysis on A.I. in the public interest.

Brennan: Here’s what I see as the biggest risk: These companies are spending so much money on building out this technology. The consulting firm Bain estimates that by 2031, they will have to achieve $6 trillion of revenue annually to sustain their current level of capital expenditure, which is $1.5 trillion a year. In order for those numbers to add up in any way, they need to push this tech everywhere, into all of our public institutions and contracting, including in areas where A.I. is not fit for purpose, is not secure, safe by design. That’s what we should be talking about.

Brennan: Government is supposed to stop harmful products from entering the market. We do it with drugs. We do it with airplanes. The issue here is corporate negligence. That should be the focus.

title: A.I.’s Rogue Behavior Starts With Its Training
content:
But security researchers pointed out that the Hugging Face breach was largely preventable with standard cybersecurity protocols. Boyan Milanov, a senior research scientist at the AI Now Institute who specializes in evaluating A.I.’s cybersecurity risks, said safety must be enforced by “having a properly designed test environment that doesn’t allow the agent’s program to perform the actions that are unwanted and potentially harmful.”

Experts argue that the inherent difficulty of containment — because of imperfect sandboxes or agents taking unintended actions — does not absolve companies of responsibility. “The rogue A.I. narrative is so useful for these companies because it absolves them from the responsibility in these incidents,” Mr. Milanov said.
